panels.title: The Company-state constitutional problem
ascii_lines: LONDON COMPANY -> shareholders, directors, trade and patronage
INDIAN SOVEREIGN -> revenue, war, justice and legislation after Diwani
CONTRADICTION -> private profit joined to public coercive power
PARLIAMENTARY RESPONSE -> regulate, supervise, centralise and finally transfer rule.
MUST REMEMBER: Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, Charter Acts 1813, 1833 and 1853,
and Government of India Act 1858 changed different corporate, executive, legislative and
patronage arrangements.
source_references: 1. A private corporation as revenue, war and justice authority
2. The crisis that forced Parliament to act, 1770-73: fiscal, political, and patronage -- not humanitarian

panels.title: Regulating Act 1773: first framework
ascii_lines: GOVERNOR-GENERAL OF BENGAL + COUNCIL OF FOUR -> Warren Hastings first
BOMBAY / MADRAS -> subordinated in war and peace, with practical ambiguities
SUPREME COURT AT CALCUTTA -> begins 1774 under Crown-appointed judges
DIRECTORS REPORT TO MINISTRY -> oversight begins, but Company rule continues.
source_references: 3. The Regulating Act, 1773: institutions on paper

panels.title: Why the 1773 design malfunctioned
ascii_lines: COUNCIL ARITHMETIC -> Francis-Clavering-Monson majority can outvote Hastings
JURISDICTIONAL OVERLAP -> Supreme Court clashes with Company revenue and civil courts
CASES -> Nand Kumar, Patna and Cossijurah expose uncertainty
LESSON -> constitutional repair follows administrative conflict, not a smooth master plan.
source_references: 4. Why the Regulating Act failed in practice: the Hastings-Council deadlock
5. The Supreme Court and jurisdictional conflict: Nand Kumar, Patna, Cossijurah

panels.title: Amending Act 1781: targeted jurisdictional repair
ascii_lines: BEFORE -> official acts and revenue matters exposed to disputed Court reach
1781 -> official public acts exempted; revenue jurisdiction excluded
PERSONAL LAW -> Hindu and Muslim law to guide relevant cases
LIMIT -> corrected Court-executive conflict, not the Council voting problem.
source_references: 6. The Amending Act (Act of Settlement), 1781: precise corrections, not a general fix

panels.title: Pitt's India Act 1784: dual control in Britain
ascii_lines: COURT OF DIRECTORS -> commerce, appointments and routine Company administration
BOARD OF CONTROL -> Crown-supervised political, military and revenue direction
INDIA -> stronger Bengal control over presidencies and smaller executive council
VERDICT -> supervision without immediate Crown takeover.
source_references: 7. Pitt's India Act, 1784: Board of Control, dual government, and stronger central command

panels.title: Executive consolidation, 1786-1793
ascii_lines: 1786 -> Cornwallis may override council in special cases and serve as commander
1793 -> override power generalised to future governors-general and governors
1793 -> Company monopoly renewed for twenty years
DIRECTION -> stronger personal executive within a still Company-run constitution.
source_references: 8. The Act of 1786 and Charter Act, 1793: executive authority and continuity

panels.title: Charter Act 1813: partial commercial opening
ascii_lines: ENDED -> Company monopoly over Indian trade
RETAINED -> tea monopoly and trade with China
ADDED -> Crown sovereignty claim, missionary entry and education provision
MEANING -> British industrial access expands while the Company remains territorial ruler.
source_references: 9. Charter Act, 1813: free trade, missions, education, and a partial opening

panels.title: Charter Act 1833: all-India centralisation
ascii_lines: GG OF BENGAL -> GOVERNOR-GENERAL OF INDIA; William Bentinck first
PRESIDENCY LEGISLATURES -> legislative power centralised in the Government of India
LAW MEMBER + LAW COMMISSION -> Macaulay and codification drive
COMPANY COMMERCE ENDS -> corporation becomes a purely administrative agency.
source_references: 10. Charter Act, 1833: all-India centralisation, the Law Member, and codification

panels.title: The 1833 equality promise and practice gap
ascii_lines: STATUTORY LANGUAGE -> Indians not to be excluded from Company office by identity
INSTITUTIONAL REALITY -> patronage and racial barriers remain
EXAM DISTINCTION -> 1833 voices open eligibility; it does not create the 1853 exam
ANALYTICAL USE -> liberal language coexists with an unrepresentative imperial state.
source_references: 11. Charter Act, 1833: the non-discrimination promise and the practice gap

panels.title: Charter Act 1853: legislature and recruitment
ascii_lines: EXECUTIVE COUNCIL -> legislative members added for a distinct law-making function
CENTRAL LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL -> procedure resembles a small official parliament
OPEN COMPETITION -> civil-service recruitment principle implemented through later rules
LIMIT -> London examination and access barriers make formal openness unequal in practice.
CLOSE DISTINCTION: Distinguish enactment from commencement and policy from implementation: the
1833 Act ended Company commerce, while open competitive recruitment developed through later
measures.
source_references: 12. Charter Act, 1853: legislative-executive separation and the civil-service reform sequence, 1833-1855

panels.title: Government of India Act 1858: transfer, not reinvention
ascii_lines: ABOLISHED -> Company rule, Court of Directors and Board of Control
CREATED -> Secretary of State for India assisted by an India Council
INDIA -> Governor-General also becomes Viceroy; Canning first
CONTINUITY -> central executive, councils, codes and bureaucracy largely survive transfer.
EVIDENCE LIMIT: Read statutory text with Company practice and parliamentary inquiry;
constitutional centralisation did not remove distance, discretion, corruption or racial
exclusion.
source_references: 13. The Government of India Act, 1858: transfer to the Crown, Secretary of State, India Council, and Viceroy

panels.title: Constitutional ladder, 1773-1858
ascii_lines: 1773 OVERSIGHT -> 1781 JURISDICTIONAL REPAIR -> 1784 CROWN SUPERVISION
1813 MONOPOLY BREACH -> 1833 CENTRAL GOVERNMENT + CODIFICATION
1853 LEGISLATIVE SPECIALISATION + COMPETITIVE RECRUITMENT
1858 CROWN RULE -> sovereign changes; colonial centralisation remains.
source_references: 14. Institutional themes across 1773-1858: centralisation, codification, bureaucracy, and exclusion
15. Historiography of the Company-state: three readings and a defensible synthesis
16. Comparative synthesis: the constitutional ladder, provision-to-effect table, and answer architecture
